Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

AURORA, Colorado (CNN) -- The Atlanta lawyer with tuberculosis who caused an international health scare after traveling to Europe and back underwent surgery Tuesday to remove the diseased portion of one of his lungs. TB patient Andrew Speaker set off an international health scare when he traveled to Europe for his wedding in May. Andrew Speaker, 31, had the roughly two-hour operation to remove the upper lobe of his right lung at the University of Colorado Hospital. He's been under treatment at National Jewish Medical and Research Center in Denver since the end of May. CNN's Dr. Sanjay Gupta, who observed the surgery for about an hour, explained that the unusual procedure consisted of inserting a video camera in a tube in one small incision in the right side of Speaker's chest, and putting instruments through another incision. When the infected portion of the lung was cut out, it was placed inside a bag while still inside the attorney's chest cavity and the bag was sealed inside a tube before being removed. The main reason for sealing the infected tissue was to prevent it from re-infecting Speaker as it was removed, Gupta said after the operation. Doctors also wanted to make sure they didn't "release any of that tuberculosis bacteria into the operating room, into the rest of the hospital," Gupta said before the surgery on CNN's "American Morning." Watch Andrew Speaker discuss his reasons for having surgery with CNN's Dr. Sanjay Gupta » . Doctors said the operation went well and there was not much bleeding, Gupta said. The portion of the lung that was removed showed the effects of the disease, Gupta said. "A regular lung is very pink with a smooth, glistening surface," he said. "This had a lot of bumps on it, and the areas that were diseased were very dark with white nodules." Speaker will most likely recover at the University of Colorado Hospital for another couple of days, and will return to National Jewish Medical and Research Center in Denver to finish his antibiotic course. He will still have to continue taking the medications prescribed by his doctors to fight the tuberculosis until cultures taken from him are negative for tuberculosis bacteria for eight weeks. At that point, he will be considered non-infectious, but he will still be monitored by health care professionals. Speaker said it was his decision to have the surgery, which is just one of his treatment options. "With the amount of treatment I'm going to be on, the doctors said if you go ahead and have this surgery, you don't have to worry 10 years from now, or 20 years from now, or 30 years from now if it's ever going to come back, so it's worth the peace of mind to me," the attorney said. Speaker was originally found to have an extremely drug resistant strain (XDR-TB) of the respiratory disease earlier this year, but on July 3 doctors said he had multi-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), which is treatable with less toxic drugs. Speaker and his fiancee had gone to Europe on May 12 for their wedding in Greece, despite warnings from the Fulton County Health Department in Georgia that he should not fly because he risked infecting fellow passengers. Since then, eight people who shared a flight with Speaker have filed a lawsuit against him, seeking $1.3 million in damages. Rosalind Yee -- an attorney for the plaintiffs who said her clients include a ninth person related to one of the passengers but who was not on the flight -- said all eight passengers have undergone TB tests since they returned home. One of them, a 72-year-old man, tested positive for TB on a skin test, though it was not clear that Speaker was the source. The man's X-rays were normal, she said, and he is awaiting results of further tests. In the past year, there have been about 124 cases of MDR-TB in the United States. About half of those patients have elected to undergo the surgery to remove the diseased portion of their lungs, Gupta said. E-mail to a friend .

AURORA, Colorado (CNN) — An Atlanta attorney diagnosed with tuberculosis, whose trip to Europe and return to the United States prompted an international public-health alarm, had surgery Tuesday to take out the affected section of one lung.

Andrew Speaker, the 31-year-old TB patient whose May travel to Europe for his wedding drew worldwide attention, underwent an operation lasting about two hours at the University of Colorado Hospital. Surgeons removed the upper lobe of his right lung. Since late May, Speaker has been receiving care at the National Jewish Medical and Research Center in Denver.

CNN medical correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta, who watched roughly an hour of the procedure, said the operation was uncommon. Surgeons made a small incision on the right side of Speaker’s chest and inserted a tube containing a video camera, while surgical tools were passed through a second incision.

After the diseased lung tissue was removed, doctors put it into a bag while it was still inside Speaker’s chest cavity. The bag was then closed inside a tube before being taken out. Gupta said afterward that the infected tissue was sealed mainly to keep it from reintroducing infection into Speaker’s body during removal. Before the procedure, Gupta also said on CNN’s “American Morning” that physicians wanted to avoid releasing tuberculosis bacteria into the operating room or elsewhere in the hospital.

Doctors reported that the surgery was successful and involved little bleeding, Gupta said. He added that the removed lung tissue clearly showed damage from the illness. A normal lung, Gupta explained, is bright pink with a smooth, shiny surface. By contrast, the removed tissue had many bumps, and the diseased areas were dark and marked with white nodules.

Speaker is expected to remain at the University of Colorado Hospital for a few more days before returning to the National Jewish Medical and Research Center in Denver to complete his antibiotic treatment. He must keep taking the medications ordered by his doctors until cultures taken from him remain negative for tuberculosis bacteria for eight weeks. Once that happens, he will be considered no longer infectious, though medical professionals will continue monitoring him.

Speaker said he chose surgery himself, noting that it was only one possible treatment path. He said doctors told him that, given the length and intensity of his treatment, surgery could help eliminate concerns that the disease might return years later. For him, he said, that reassurance made the operation worthwhile.

Earlier in the year, Speaker was initially believed to have an extensively drug-resistant form of tuberculosis, known as XDR-TB. However, on July 3, doctors said he instead had multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, or MDR-TB, a form that can be treated with medications that are less toxic.

Speaker and his fiancée left for Europe on May 12 for their wedding in Greece, even though Georgia’s Fulton County Health Department had warned him not to fly because he might infect other passengers. Since then, eight people who were on a flight with Speaker have sued him, asking for $1.3 million in damages.

Rosalind Yee, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said her clients also include a ninth person who is related to one of the passengers but was not on the flight. According to Yee, all eight passengers were tested for TB after returning home. One passenger, a 72-year-old man, had a positive TB skin test, although it was not known whether Speaker was the source. Yee said the man’s X-rays were normal and that he was waiting for additional test results.

Gupta said that in the past year, the United States has recorded about 124 cases of MDR-TB. Roughly half of those patients have chosen surgery to remove the diseased part of their lungs.

## Andrew Speaker TB Case: Diagnosis, Colorado Surgery and Passenger Lawsuit Revisited

**ATLANTA/DENVER —** Andrew Speaker, the Atlanta attorney whose 2007 international travel triggered one of the most widely publicized tuberculosis scares in recent U.S. history, became the focus of global attention after health officials said he had traveled on commercial flights while infected with a drug-resistant form of TB.

Speaker’s case raised urgent questions about public-health authority, airline passenger notification, patient responsibility and the risks posed by multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, commonly known as **MDR-TB**.

### Diagnosis before wedding trip

Speaker was diagnosed in 2007 with tuberculosis before leaving the United States for a planned wedding trip to Europe. Health officials later said laboratory testing indicated he had a drug-resistant strain of the disease. At different points in the case, officials publicly described the infection as **multidrug-resistant TB** and later as an even more serious form, **extensively drug-resistant TB**, or XDR-TB. Subsequent testing reportedly led specialists to conclude that his infection was MDR-TB rather than XDR-TB.

MDR-TB is resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin, the two most powerful first-line TB drugs. It is more difficult and time-consuming to treat than ordinary tuberculosis, often requiring prolonged therapy with second-line medications.

Speaker has said he did not believe he was contagious when he traveled and that he was not explicitly ordered not to fly before leaving the United States. Public-health officials, however, said he had been advised against travel because of the potential risk to others.

### International travel sparks alarm

Despite the diagnosis, Speaker traveled overseas for his wedding and honeymoon. His itinerary included flights from the United States to Europe and later a return route through Canada. The case escalated after U.S. officials sought to prevent him from taking another commercial flight back into the country.

Speaker ultimately flew from Prague to Montreal and then entered the United States by car. He was later placed under a federal isolation order — a rarely used public-health measure — and was treated in specialized medical facilities.

The incident prompted the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to work with airlines and foreign health authorities to locate passengers who may have been seated near Speaker on the relevant flights. Public-health agencies generally consider prolonged exposure in enclosed spaces, such as aircraft cabins, a potential risk factor for TB transmission, though casual contact does not automatically result in infection.

### Treatment and surgery at University of Colorado Hospital

Speaker eventually received care in Colorado, where specialists evaluated the extent of his disease and treatment options. In July 2007, he underwent lung surgery at **University of Colorado Hospital** in Aurora.

Doctors removed diseased lung tissue as part of his treatment plan. Surgery is not routine for all TB patients, but it may be considered in select drug-resistant TB cases when infection is localized and when removing damaged or infected tissue could improve the chances of cure alongside antibiotic therapy.

After the operation, physicians reported that Speaker was recovering and that his prognosis was favorable. He continued treatment with anti-tuberculosis medications under medical supervision.

### Passengers sue over exposure fears

The case also moved into the courts. Passengers who had flown on the same commercial aircraft as Speaker filed lawsuits alleging they had been exposed to a dangerous communicable disease and suffered fear, anxiety, inconvenience and medical-monitoring costs.

The lawsuits focused particularly on passengers aboard the transatlantic flight Speaker took while returning from Europe through Canada. Plaintiffs argued that they were forced to undergo TB testing and endure uncertainty about whether they had contracted a serious drug-resistant infection.

The legal claims reflected a broader debate over liability in public-health scares: whether an infected traveler can be held responsible for flying, what warnings were given, and what damages passengers may recover when exposure creates fear but does not necessarily result in illness.

Public reports at the time indicated that health authorities did not identify widespread transmission linked to Speaker’s flights. TB is transmitted through airborne particles, but infection typically requires sufficient exposure to an infectious person, and not every person with TB is equally contagious.

### A landmark public-health controversy

Speaker’s case became a landmark example of the tension between individual mobility and infectious-disease control in an era of global air travel. It led to scrutiny of how health agencies communicate with patients, how quickly no-fly warnings can be implemented, and how governments coordinate across borders when a potentially infectious traveler is already abroad.

Although Speaker survived and continued treatment, the controversy surrounding his travel, diagnosis, surgery and the passenger lawsuits left a lasting imprint on public-health policy discussions — particularly concerning drug-resistant tuberculosis and the legal tools available to prevent possible exposure during international travel.
